project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The stream is currently used as internal fuel, so diverting it to a saleable product would affect the mill's existing fuel route.
There is no lignin dryer, so buyers requiring dry powder would need drying before shipment or use.
Solvent or membrane fractionation is not available, limiting routes that require fractionated lignin.
Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting routes that require in-house functionalization.
The stream leaves as wet cake, so moisture increases shipped mass and must be managed by prospective buyers.
Covered cake storage is limited, constraining inventory buffering.
Missing composition and property data prevent reliable screening against pathway or buyer specifications.
Moisture is uncertain, so actual dry output and shipping mass may differ from the profile.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional_demo: the mill, stream, and all values are invented illustrative assumptions, not measurements from a real mill.
The profile must be replaced with mill production records and laboratory data before any commercial decision.
Lignin, ash, sulfur, carbohydrate, molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium data are missing; composition total was therefore not checked.
The lignin analytical method is stated for illustration and needs confirmation before comparison with buyer specifications.
Moisture is marked uncertain and should be measured over time rather than treated as a fixed value.
The recorded dry-matter balance passes: 26000.0 t/yr is consistent with the wet quantity and moisture inputs.
agent.summary: Validated fictional profile: 40000.0 t/yr wet kraft lignin cake at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003, yielding 26000.0 t/yr dry mass; the record passes balance checks but is not decision-ready because key composition data are missing and the stream is wet, internally consumed, and unsupported by drying or downstream processing equipment.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin has been reported for veneer plywood, with UPM stating industrial proof and EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 performance.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include plywood manufacturers and producers of wood-based panels that use phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A documented plywood application meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3, and formaldehyde emissions were measured using EN 717-2.
One laboratory study assessed resin viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard.

limitations: Evidence includes vendor technical literature and laboratory studies, not a buyer-validated assessment of Pinecrest lignin cake.
The cited depolymerized-lignin molecular-weight range is not established as a delivered-feedstock requirement.
The reported market forecast has no attached forecast year, and the market value is from 2019.
missing_information: No lignin price, purchase volume, named buyer, contract structure, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence establishes Pinecrest cake composition, ash, moisture, or suitability for the required activation or depolymerization process.
No evidence quantifies the cost of drying or pretreatment for wet cake.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents industrially proven LPF resin performance and established wood-panel use, but it does not document commercial sales by multiple producers or named buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been investigated as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane and polyisocyanurate foams.

Unmodified lignin has been tested as a replacement for petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam; kraft lignins produced denser and stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The broader lignin-polyurethane pathway includes foams, panels, coatings, and rubber replacement.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid insulation-foam producers and other polyurethane foam manufacturers.
Potential customers for flexible foam include manufacturers of heavy-duty foam products.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: A study cited total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups, as an acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production.
In one study, rigid foams with 19-23% hardwood kraft lignin by weight retained comparable structure and strength.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties.
Rigid foam qualification was assessed against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications in one laboratory study.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies, and the pathway review rates lignin polyurethane uses at TRL 6 rather than demonstrating commercial kraft-lignin production.
Performance varies by lignin type; the best rigid-foam performer in one study was not kraft lignin.
The flexible-foam study compared laboratory foams with automotive OEM requirements, but odor was not measured.
A review abstract identifies low consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs as commercialization barriers.
missing_information: No lignin price, purchase volume, named buyer, contract structure, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence establishes Pinecrest cake's total hydroxyl value, moisture, ash, sulfur, or viscosity behavior in polyol.
No evidence demonstrates performance using wet kraft lignin cake or identifies a commercial drying and modification route.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research interest and pathway-level development, including laboratory testing and a TRL assessment, but it does not document commercial sales, named buyers, or development partnerships for Pinecrest-type kraft lignin.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.

applications.statement: Lignin can serve as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the evidence describes demanding precursor specifications and purification needs.
Lignin-derived hard carbon is documented for sodium-ion battery anodes, including hard carbon made from kraft lignin.
Lignin can be converted to activated carbon, including when its impurity level makes it unsuitable for other carbon-material uses.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include carbon-fiber precursor and carbon-fiber manufacturers.
Potential customers include sodium-ion battery anode-material producers and battery manufacturers.

competing_materials.statement: The named incumbent for carbon fiber is PAN-based carbon fiber.
Named comparison feedstocks for sodium-ion battery hard carbon include anthracite and cellulose.
Conventional activated carbon is the competing material for the activated-carbon application.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99% and ash below 0.1% by weight.
The cited carbon-fiber specification requires residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and complete removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber required purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing agent for melt spinning.
For activated carbon, the evidence reports no strict precursor-quality limitation, while lower ash improves yield.
Battery-material qualification may require engagement with battery manufacturers and carmakers; one company states that qualification can take 3 years.

limitations: Carbon fiber evidence is based partly on specifications cited secondhand and on studies using non-kraft lignin or older work.
Hard-carbon evidence is a review of sodium-ion battery studies, while the battery-company evidence concerns lithium-ion anode material and includes forward-looking company statements.
Activated-carbon evidence is laboratory-scale and uses zinc chloride activation.
Modeled carbon-fiber costs and project scale-up claims are not measured commercial results.
missing_information: No lignin price, purchase volume, named Pinecrest buyer, contract structure, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence establishes Pinecrest cake's ash, sulfur, carbohydrate, moisture, volatile, metal, or particle-size values against carbon-fiber or battery specifications.
No evidence provides qualification specifications for Pinecrest material in hard-carbon or activated-carbon products.
No evidence quantifies the cost or availability of drying, purification, activation, carbonization, or other required processing for Pinecrest cake.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents development activity, including a validated industrially relevant precursor-fiber environment, a battery-material pilot line, and manufacturer qualification activity, but it does not document established commercial sales to several buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin would need activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
The wet cake would need moisture management and likely drying before shipment or use because the mill has no lignin dryer.
Customer qualification would need to address plywood bonding performance and formaldehyde emissions, with documented evidence using EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and EN 717-2 methods.

technical_maturity.statement: Biobased phenolic-resin production is reported at TRL 8, which the readiness assessment maps to a technical-readiness score of 5.

adoption_barriers.statement: Pinecrest lacks the chemical-modification equipment needed for the required activation or depolymerization, so commercialization would require an external processor, new equipment, or a buyer that performs the treatment.
Composition, ash, sulfur, moisture, molecular weight, and hydroxyl data are missing, preventing reliable screening against resin specifications and buyer requirements.
The route must compete with phenol and secure plywood or wood-panel customers willing to qualify a lignin-containing adhesive.

The economics are indicative only and cannot establish profitability without yield, price, and variable-cost inputs.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: The pathway is technically mature and has identifiable plywood and wood-panel customers, but Pinecrest needs pretreatment and moisture management that are not available in the mill's current assets; commercialization is therefore feasible with significant investment or a processing/customer partner.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 8 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-01#3.

main_drivers: Attractiveness is indicative at 2.73, with a range of 1.95–3.75, but only 0.55 of the scoring weight is assessed.
Technical readiness is score 3 and market evidence is score 3, supported by development activity, a pilot-line context, and manufacturer qualification activity.
Commercialization feasibility is score 2 because purification and carbon-processing capabilities, plus demanding customer qualification, are not identified.
Feedstock compatibility and indicative economics are unassessed; evidence quality is high overall, with three high-quality and two moderate-quality cited records.
what_could_change_it: Measured ash, lignin, sulfur, carbohydrate, moisture, volatile, metal, and particle-size data matched to a defined carbon-material specification could establish feedstock compatibility and move the pathway up or down.
A defined product route—activated carbon, hard carbon, or carbon fiber—with demonstrated yield, product price, and variable costs could establish economics and materially change its position.
A named buyer, qualification specification, processing partner, and demonstrated pilot product could improve commercialization feasibility; adverse qualification or processing results could lower it.

A named plywood or wood-panel buyer accepting Pinecrest cake and its activation or depolymerization route could improve feasibility; failed resin qualification or unfavorable diversion costs could lower it.

validation_steps.action: Obtain a representative Pinecrest cake campaign sample and measure moisture, lignin, ash, sulfur, carbohydrates, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl, sodium, total hydroxyl value, metals, volatiles, and particle size.
validation_steps.reason: This fills the missing feedstock profile and enables compatibility screening rather than treating unassessed criteria as poor performance.

validation_steps.action: Run bench-scale drying and pathway-specific pretreatment trials for resin, polyurethane, and the selected carbon-material route; record mass balance, energy use, processing yield, and product properties.
validation_steps.reason: This tests the stated wet-cake, drying, pretreatment, and processing constraints and supplies the yield and variable-cost inputs currently missing.

validation_steps.action: Define one product specification and obtain customer or processor quotations covering purchase volume, price, acceptance tests, contract structure, and qualification requirements.
validation_steps.reason: The pathways currently lack comparable buyer, demand, pricing, and qualification evidence; a defined product is necessary because the carbon pathway spans different applications.

validation_steps.action: Build a complete contribution model for each selected route, including product yield, product price, drying, pretreatment, modification, purification, carbon processing, logistics, and the opportunity cost of diverting lignin from internal fuel.
validation_steps.reason: The scoring engine could not assess economics, and the mill's existing fuel route is a material commercial constraint.

validation_steps.action: Conduct qualification trials with the leading customer or processing partner and document TRL, scale-up requirements, asset ownership, and timing to commercial operation.
validation_steps.reason: This distinguishes technical maturity from actual Pinecrest commercialization readiness and tests whether the required partner and assets can be secured.

ranking_changers: A measured feedstock profile matched to numeric pathway requirements, especially ash, moisture, lignin content, hydroxyl functionality, sulfur, and particle size.
Product-specific yield, price, and variable-cost data, including drying and pretreatment or carbon-processing costs; these would populate the currently unassessed economics criterion.
A named buyer or processor with a purchase volume, qualification specification, and commercial acceptance decision.
Evidence on the opportunity cost and operational impact of diverting the stream from internal fuel.
For carbon materials, selecting and validating one product route rather than combining carbon fiber, hard carbon, and activated carbon in one pathway.
caveats: All three pathways are listed as insufficient data, so score_and_rank assigned no ranks and did not produce a ranked ordering.
The attractiveness values and ranges are indicative, not ranks; feedstock compatibility and indicative economics were unassessed for every pathway because required inputs were missing.
The Pinecrest feedstock profile is fictional, and its moisture and composition are not established.
The assessment does not calculate profitability, net present value, capital expenditure, life-cycle impacts, or a complete diversion opportunity cost.
Technical-readiness evidence is pathway-level and may not represent a qualified product made from Pinecrest wet kraft lignin cake.
report.summary: Phenolic resins have the strongest indicative attractiveness and technical-readiness signal, carbon materials are intermediate with substantial route-specific uncertainty, and polyurethanes have the weakest indicative signal. However, none can be ranked until feedstock compatibility and economics are assessed. The next decision should focus on representative testing, a defined product and buyer, and a mass-balance and cost model that includes drying, processing, qualification, logistics, and the internal-fuel diversion.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
